ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to disable New User login?
ResponsesInList.Text: -If- you have accounts for users that are established in an LDAP server , you could set authentication to LDAP. -Then- only people who are 'registered' in LDAP will be able to 'check in' to your Moodle site. (I'm using Windows 2000 Active Directory -which uses LDAP-; you could use Novell or others as well.)  If a student is not already registered in Moodle, the first time they 'check in' they will have to fill in the New User form; I avoid that by uploading all students into Moodle (using the Upload User feature). I see Registering students in Moodle as only the first step. We also control Enrollment in courses; we do not allow self-enrollment. To accomplish this, we first insure that we have enrolled every student in at least one course (also using the Upload User feature).  Then we don't provide a means for users to get to a Course List (don't show the Courses block, and set Site Settings -> Front Page Format to "Show List of Courses - then they see only the courses they've been enrolled in).  We chose to not set up Enrollment Keys for (all the) courses, tho' that is probably a more reliable method to prevent self-enrollments.

ResponsesInList.Title: With Force Change Password, user cannot leave change_password.php without logging out?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, I'm having a problem when the user's account is forced to change its password.  After the user gets directed to change_password.php, and successfully changes the password, he cannot leave that page.  Any other page he tries to go to will send him back to change_password.php again. I tracked it down and the problem seems to be that the unset_user_preference function deletes the auth_forcechangepassword preference from the database , but doesn't unset it in $USER->preference["auth_forcechangepassword"].  So any other page that requires a login will check against the $USER object, sees that the user still has to change the password, and redirects back to change_password.php. Is this true for all Moodle 1.5 installs, or did we break something on our local site without realizing it? And if it is true for all Moodle installs, shouldn't the unset_user_preference function also unset the preference in $USER as well as taking it out of the db? Thanks, Jim Stoner

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: move to LDAP authentication from the E-mail
ResponsesInList.Text: Assuming the username in moodle matches the username in ldap, you could change the individual accounts to use LDAP authentication instead of manual (it's just a single field in their user record in the moodle db).  When we moved from database authentication to ldap I just did a big update of the table and the existing people all worked.  Since their moodle id value is unchanged all of their courses will be unchanged as well. But if the usernames don't match, you could change the individual accounts in the database (depending on how many changes you need to do) to match. If you just do a switch for the site to LDAP, then the previous accounts will still exist and new LDAP ones will be created unless the usernames overlap (I think).  Courses are tied to the moodle id value of the user so new accounts will have new moodle id values and different courses. --S

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Active Directory Authentication Problem
ResponsesInList.Text: utf8_decode is part of PHP's XML libraries, and it seems they are missing on your system. The solution is, naturally, to install them ;) Probably your linux distribution has them prepackaged. There'll be a php4-xml RPM/Deb package to install. Without XML support, many things in Moodle will be broken, for example backup & restore.

ResponsesInList.Title: A halfway house between MS-SQL user database & Moodle to solve authentication problems?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello! Here's my situation... We have a user database (used for lots of other things) in MS- SQL Server . Trying to set Moodle up to authenticate against this yields a big flat blank. Nothing. Nada. Zilch. See here and here ... So here's my plan... I'd like to establish something - a (probably Open Source) server holding a database - which can act as an intermediary between the two systems. Once the MS-SQL server authentication is sorted we can remove this "middle (wo)man" but here's how I'd envisage it worked... 1. Moodle server ( MySQL / PHP / IIS ) 1. authenticates against 2. using 'Moodle-friendly' database running on 2. » 2. New intermediate server (running ???) « query from 3. creates up-to-date view of user database on 2. 3. User database (MS-SQL Server) - currently "Moodle authentication unfriendly" The new intermediary would query the MS-SQL user database every n minutes / seconds and hold a 'view' of the database which was as up to date as n was. Users logging on to Moodle would be authenticated against this view, which would (we hope) be an accurate reflection of the user database. Does anyone have any thoughts on what I could use to achieve this in a straightforward and robust way - if the answer's MySQL then that's fine, but I'd like to know about something that will be as flexible and robust as possible when it comes up against the MS-SQL Server... ...also, if I've missed the point completely, please put me right. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: A halfway house between MS-SQL user database & Moodle to solve authentication problems?
ResponsesInList.Text: Well, you can, of course. If you are going to do it, put the data directly in a different mysql database (on the same db server) and you're done. It'll give you better performance and reduce dependencies. Now, if your export/import scripts are doing any data transformation, you may think of updating the moodle user table directly, and skip the intermediate step. You problem wit MSSQL , however, is probably easy to resolve. Has PHP got the MSSQL extensions installed? What error do you get in error.log?

ResponsesInList.Title: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text: As part of the NZVLE project, I've been working with Mark Jones to create an integration with the Artena SMS -- a popular product here in New Zealand. The code is licensed under the GPL, and you can download the preview release artena_sms-pre_01 from Eduforge. Or you can get it from Moodle's contrib/artena_sms directory. Check out the release notes , too. It contains two parts: a C# .NET app that exports from Artena to a really generic XML file format (check the sample_data directory) a set of Perl scripts that validate and import that data automagically into a Postgres database for use as DB backend to Moodle's auth/db and enrol/db modules A third part is coming as improvements & bugfixes to the auth/db and enrol/db plugins to make them as smart as the LDAP plugins. Proper field locks for user fields are part of it (in 1.5 already). Other bits will be merged as soon as they are ready (and 1.5 is out the door naturally). This setup exports from the SMS to Moodle a listing of student records a listing of current courses a listing of current enrolments You can, of course, extend the approach to exchange more data -- tutor/staff accounts, tutor-course relations, assessment data, etc. And there are ways for Moodle to feed data back to the SMS. We haven't gone so far with Artena yet (we have with other SMSs -- Artena internals aren't too friendly to that kind of manipulation). We are hoping that this is useful and helps open the door for other interesting SMS integration projects. This is working code for a medium-complexity SMS integration -- based on our experience integrating Moodle with other SMSs -- and still very readable.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text: You should consider using the IMS Enterprise ( www.imsproject.org/enterprise ) for your XML . Everything you are doing can be represented in it. The advantage is now you are working in standard data schema, one that is used across multiple SIS and LMS products. We have done this at University of Wisconsin. 14 SIS, 9 of which are PeopleSoft. All emit the same XML. From there, it's a short step to a Web Services implementation. Instead of generating XML files for the entire dataset, you send just incremental updates. The Web Services does also provide for error handling, which is more complex in a real-time updating mode. IMS Enterprise Services defines how to do this.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Dirk, I'm interested if you can upload the info or send it to me. We're just about to start a Banner->Moodle integration, and we'd like to make it in such a way that it can be applicable as possible to Peoplesoft and Fusion integrations we'll need to do in the future.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text:
Dirk, I am well aware of the IMS Enterprise set if schemas. Feel free to use this code we have made available (have you looked at it?) and improve it to use your XML schema of choice. Patches are welcome. I do have a LOT more detail on how we did this at UW, if you are
interested I'll upload. Code is better than detail ;) Perhaps a directory in /contrib for your export scripts and sample XML files?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text: I guess I should explain my hot-headed reply a bit better ;) This is an example of a simple initial approach to SMS integration. Part of the reason is a KISS mantra, another part is that the access we have to the Artena internals is limited, and Artena itself seems to be storing less data than we'd like to. So our limits were marked by Artena itself, or our ability to export from it. No staff data, not record modification timestamps (to do incremental transfers) and no feeding data back to the SMS either. With other SMS we have done all these things -- and this ends up being really powerful but invariably tied to the SMS internals. In this case the integration ended up being simple and rather SMS-neutral. And I think that makes it really interesting as a starting point for other integration efforts. WRT IMS Enterprise, I have been evaluating it as of late, and I find it so-so. The schemas are simple and would support this kind of limited integration, but much more. The standard is not very stable: it has changed formats 3 times already, and names once, all in a short period of time. So it's the standard du jour ... and I tend to take my time to judge those ;) But the real issue with IMS Enterprise and similar standards is that when I sit down to design a complex SMS integration job, they are not applicable, because we are mapping things much closer to the internals of SMS and LMS. Yes, we forfeit portability, but we integrate into the institutions workflow -- for systems that they are planning on running for a few years.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text: With other SMS we have done all these things Hi Martin, did the other SMS include Banner or Peoplesoft? We're about to try and improve on our Banner integration and we'd like to do it in a way that would be as easy as possible to port to Peoplesoft, do you have any experience and/or code for these integrations?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text: Haven't worked with either Banner or PeopleSoft. I think we'll be working with Banner soon as a local uni here is an Oracle shop, and they are part of the NZVLE consortium. If you happen to go with Banner before we do, I'm interested in hearing how it goes

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Student Management System integration - Artena sample
ResponsesInList.Text: Our experience in the UW has shown that's it useful to adopt a single exchange format. We have multiple SISs, with the largest number being PeopleSoft. For the PS campuses, the datafeed code was provided to them. For other campuses, they had a clear target to shoot at. What I'm suggesting is that there is virtue in a universal exchange format. You are saying it costs to much to do this for a particular implementaton. I'm saying it costs less, over all the implementations, as you will have cost savings for those that can leverage the work of others in a more universal way.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: LDAP, Active Directory, and Missing Info
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Mark, Yes, with a little bit of effort, I was able to accomplish Active Directory-Moodle integration.  Here's how to do it . . . Under "Administration," choose "Authentication."  In the "Choose an authentication method:" drop-down, choose "Use an LDAP Server ."  The settings will then appear.  Next, you need to fill out these Settings. In the "ldap_host_url:" field, enter in the fully-qualified domain name of your server with Active Directory installed on it, proceeding it with "ldap://".  For example, if the name of your server was "myserver," and your domain was "myorganization.com," then this blank would read: ldap://myserver.myorganization.com In the "ldap_contexts:" field, you need to enter in the locations of where you stored all of your users in LDAP-style format.  Let's say that you had, for example, created an organizational unit called "Students" and an organizational unit called "Teachers" at the root level of your Active Directory tree.  (In other words, at the same depth as the "Users" folder.)  Then, let's say that you also had users in the "Users" folder.  Your "ldap_contexts:" field, carrying forward the previous "myorganization.com" example, would be: ou=Students,dc=myorganization,dc=com;ou=Teachers,dc=myorganization,dc=com;cn=Users,dc=myorganization,dc=com Note that the "Users" folder is prefaced with "cn=" and that all organization units you have created are prefaced with "ou=" In the "ldap_user_attribute:" field, you are entering in the specific attribute in the LDAP server that matches up with the username.  If you want your users to type in their first name and last name to login, you should be able to input "cn" if you've got their first and last names entered into Active Directory.  Chances are, though, that you want them to use their Windows username to login.  So, in this field, enter: sAMAccountName The "ldap_search_sub:" field controls whether you want to search subcontexts for the user.  If you're like me, your organizational unit called "Students" has sub-organizational units corresponding to each class.  So, for example, I have a "Students" organizational unit inside Active Directory, and, inside that, I have another organizational unit called "Class of 2006."  If you want to search such sub-organizational units for users, set the value of "ldap_search_sub:" to anything other than zero.  (1 is a good choice.) In order for you to search Active Directory via LDAP, you must login using a username and password.  This is called "binding" to the LDAP server.  So, create a user that you wish to use for binding.  This user does NOT have to be a Domain Admin.  For example, you could create a user with firstname MoodleUser and lastname MoodleUser.  Then, enter this username into the "ldap_bind_dn:" blank in LDAP format.  For example: cn=MoodleUser MoodleUser,cn=Users,dc=myorganization,dc=com In the next blank, "ldap_bind_pw:", enter in the password for the MoodleUser you just created. In the next blank, "ldap_memberattribute:", you are telling Moodle the name of the attribute in the LDAP server where it can find group membership information.  In Active Directory, this is: memberOf The next blank is "ldap_creators:".  In this blank, enter in the Active Directory groups (in LDAP style, of course) who should be imbued with the power to create courses.  If you're like me, all of the groups are located in the "Users" folder.  So, for example, to give your teachers who are members of the "Teachers" group the power to create courses, you would enter: cn=Teachers,cn=Users,dc=myorganization,dc=com I have left "ldap_create_context:" blank.  From my reading, Moodle can create users via LDAP in a particular location you specify here.  Since I want to do all user account creation myself in Active Directory, I've left this blank The next series of optional blanks involve inputting the name of the attribute in LDAP corresponding to the information requested.  If you put these in with the proper capitalization that's in Active Directory, it doesn't seem to work.  It appears that they need to be lowercase.  So, that said, they are: Firstname: givenname Lastname: sn Email address: userprincipalname or mail Phone 1: telephonenumber Phone 2: othertelephone Address: streetaddress City/town: l (that's the letter l) Countery: c Description: description ID number: useraccountcontrol I don't see anywhere in Active Directory where language is stored, so I just typed "English" in the blank.  For the email address, if your Active Directory domain matches your email address, you can just use userprincipalname.  For example, if your Active Directory is myorganization.com and your email addresses are username@myorganization.com , then userprincipal name will be fine.  If they're not the same, then enter the email addresses into the "E-mail:" blank on the "General" tab of the user's "Properties," and you should be set. Also, I don't store ID numbers in Active Directory, so I just set it to useraccountcontrol, which, I think, is a unique number given to each user account.  You could just as well leave that blank uncompleted. With all of this, I have noticed something . . . whether it's a bug or a "behaves as expected," I'm not sure.  If you enter in the data in the various fields (I think particularly the email field), the user is not prompted to edit his/her profile as under the email confirmation method.  The user is simply logged in and whatever information in Active Directory is transferred. Give it a shot and see if it works! Kyle

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle and Shibboleth
ResponsesInList.Text: Yesterday I was given a very nice demo (by the smart people at MAMS ) of a stock Moodle 1.5 installation running in a federated Shibboleth environment. Even though I helped work on the Shibboleth module, I had never actually seen it running before. Now I've seen Shibboleth in action I can really see the potential: it's very cool ... I think we'll start seeing this new capability in Moodle being used for a lot of exciting things. If you know nothing about this, Shibboleth allows a secure single-sign-on across all sorts of sites (which now includes Moodle). We could technically open up all our Moodle sites to each other and allow authenticated users from one site to access any other. In reality it'll mostly be used to allow access between smaller groups of institutions, but I'm starting to think about some sort of shibboleth.moodle.org for casual use.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle and Shibboleth
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, Shibboleth has quite some potential and I definetely can recommend you to try some demos (e.g. http://www.switch.ch/aai/demo/ contains links to other demos and the SWITCH live demo with technical explanations). As you noticed, jumping from one e-learning platform to another (e.g. from Moodle to Ilias to Blackboard to xy) is one thing that makes Shibboleth so attractive. However, Shibboleth is not only limited to e-learning stuff. Also libraries or web-shops (e.g. the Apple Store Switzerland) are also quite interested in authenticating users with Shibboleth for various reasons. Concerning the shibboleth.moodle.org idea one must keep in mind that one problem is that there are several so-called Shibboleth federations which all use Shibboleth but may use different Shibboleth attributes. Although there are thoughts about a "federation of federations" that would bring all Shibboleth federations under one common denominator, these ideas are still relatively vague.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle and Shibboleth
ResponsesInList.Text: Not sure if this has been posted up here before. Becta are piloting Shibboleth Authentication in the London Grid for Learning area (LGfL). The aim is to establish this method of AAA for secondary (and primary?) schools in the UK so that online content can be accessed anytime anywhere by pupils as long as their parent (origin) institution has licenced that content. Having Moodle "shibbolized" should help with its spread into UK schools. Maybe some provider using Moodle may want to get involved in further pilots? See http://getconnected.ngfl.gov.uk/index.php?s=workshops

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: just how modular is authentication?
ResponsesInList.Text: Currently Moodle does not support this level of granularity for authentication/user priveleges.  You can set your Moodle site to autologin guests (as for example moodle.org currently does).  Guests generally have access to view activities on a course by course basis. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: External database not updated when user changes password
ResponsesInList.Text: Normally, when you are using an external DB for authentication, you'll point users to a "password change" page outside Moodle. There's a setting in the External DB auth config page where you can put a URL . Moodle will normally not have enough privilege to change the user's password. You _can_ customize Moodle to do so -- in 1.5 you can give Moodle enough privileges that it can handle password updates with LDAP -- but it's not available out-of-the-box. When you point Moodle to an external DB, it usually means that you are already using the external DB for other services, Moodle therefore acts as a 'slave' of the external DB. The assumption is that the external db has its own update mechanisms, external to Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Invalid login

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Mixed authentication
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, it is possible. If you already have your users in your moodle database , they are authenticated using the method which is saved in their user records. However, if you want to use several authentication methods at the same time without having the users already in your moodle database, it is a bit more complicated. So the problem is to get the user data in your database using two methods at the same time. In my case I wanted to use 'manual' ans ' shibboleth ' authentication (I use 1.5 dev version). I did the following: - Configure the two authentication methods in the Moodle admin interface. Test them one after another (create some testuser for each method). - Copy the moodle/login/ directory (I named mine 'manuallogin' and 'shibbolethlogin'). - Add $CFG->auth = '#AUTHMETHOD#'; (replace #AUTHMETHOD# e.g. with 'shibboleth' or 'manual') and insert this line at the top after the 'require_once("../config.php");' in your newly created logindirectory index.php (e.g. 'shibbolethlogin/index.php'). - Modify your /moodle/index.php, e.g. look for the login-link and adapt it and/or extend it with your additional login-methods. I recommend that keep the name the directory of your main authentication method (the one your users will be using the most) as in the standardinstallation ('moodle/login'). This way your probably don't have to make so many changes in other files (e.g. logout.php is also located in '/moodle/login'). That theoretically should work (thanx to the modular structure of Moodle but I can't tell you for sure because I also made some other changes and I am still testing my configuration.

ResponsesInList.Title: PHP LDAP module not installed
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello everyone, i am a new to moodle, only been using it two days. i am trying to use ldap authentication and i was just wondering what the warning was about not having the php ldap module installed, and how i go about solving this. i would be gratefull for all the help i can.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: PHP LDAP module not installed
ResponsesInList.Text: I am a helpdesk administrator for the local school district, and I have already had the same problem, below is the documentation I wrote to accomplish this. Documentation for implementing the LDAP libraries into a compliation of PHP 1. Download Windows Binary Zip Package of PHP Version. Included in this Zip package are several folders. 2. Copy entire contets of 'dlls' to the System32 Folder 3. Make a folder entitled 'phpextensions' on the hard drive 4. Copy entire contets of 'extensions' to the 'phpextensions' folder on the hard drive 5. Open the php.ini file. It can be found in the windows base folder. 6 If GD, Scroll to step 10 7. Scroll down to a section entitled 'Paths and Directories' 8. There are two lines that read: ; Directory in which the loadable extensions (modules) reside. extension_dir = "/extensions" 9. Replace /extensions with 'c:\phpextensions' (The folder we made in step 3.) 10. Scroll down to a section entitled 'Dynamic Extensions' 11. There will be a list of extensions commented out with semi-colons, directly above that, add the line '--with-ldap' This is the GD switch that tells PHP to use the GD libraries. 12. Scroll down to a line that is commented out by a semi-colon that reads: ;extension=php_ldap.dll 13. Uncomment out that line by removing the semi-colon so it reads like: extension=php_ldap.dll 14. Save file and reload phpinfo.php script. 15. Open the Zip package of the PHP compilation and copy the entire contents over the PHP root directory. Over-write all files. 16. If phpinfo.php does not exist, create a text file and put the following line in: <?php phpinfo(); ?> 17. Save file as 'phpinfo.php' and place in root directory of web server (where php scripts are hosted) 18. Open file from web browser, and scroll down to a table that is headed by 'ldap', if the table exists, the LDAP libraries have been successfully compiled.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to Connect to MS SQL Server for User Auth

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, Moodle 1.3.5 was running without troubles using ldap v3 to log-in (Lotus Domino LDAP Directory). After the migration to 1.4.3 I received the following error: "function.ldap-read: Search: Bad search filter in ..\moodle\auth\ldap\lib.php on line 129 Moodle is running on W2K, Apache2 and PHP5. The ldap-dll was activated in the php.ini. libeay32.dll and ssleay32.dll are located in the directory \winnt\system32. My user/password was accepted, but after displaying the error-message for a second, the edit profile screen was displayed without any ldap-fields. If I re-install 1.3.5, ldap is working again. LDAP-structure: o=company,c=de ou=location1,o=company,c=de ou=location2,o=company,c=de ldap_host_url: ldap://ldap.company.de ldap_version: 3 ldap_contexts: o=company,c=de ldap_user_attribute: uid ldap_search_sub: 1 ldap_bind_dn: cn=agent signer,ou=location1,o=company,c=de ldap_bind_pw: XXX ldap_memberattribute: member ldap_objectclass: person or * ldap_creators: ldap_create_context: Do I have to use the automating sync, if all users (except the admin) are part of the ldap-directory ? ResponsesInList.Text: Is "ldap_objectclass: person or *" set to literally "person or *"? That's probably the problem; it isn't a valid LDAP construct. If it can be '*' then just leave the field empty.

ResponsesInList.Title: uploaduser.php
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm having problems getting uploaduser.php to read the file data of the text file I'm submitting. I just keep getting an "'' is not a valid field name" errors, even though the format of the text file is fine. After picking through the code and reading the PHP documentation, I discovered that problem is caused by the fact that moodle is accessed via https (port 443). In uploaduser.php, my_file_get_contents() uses fopen() to read the file data, but, according to PHP.net , fopen() can only read data from port 80. There's example code in the user-contributed notes on this page that suggests how to get around this problem.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Converting from IMAP to ldap authentification
ResponsesInList.Text: I suggest you setup a test moodle install, configured to use LDAP . Tweak it until you get it 'right', and at that point take a look at what the {prefix}user table looks like. Comparing the user table in your current and test installations will give you the hints you need to write a little perl or php script to do the migration. Backup first, of course. Good luck -- remember not to hardcode any db names or passwords in the script, so you can put it in Moodle's contrib directory for others to benefit from your effort!

ResponsesInList.Title: POP3 Authentication
ResponsesInList.Text: I spent some time trying to get POP3 authentication to work with no luck.  Finally I made the following change to the open call in auth/pop3/lib.php: $connection = imap_open($ host , $username, $password, OP_HALFOPEN); was replaced with: $connection = imap_open($host, $username, $password); This change seemed to solve all my problems.  According to the PHP documentation OP_HALFOPEN is for IMAP and NNTP servers.  There is no mention of POP3.  And it appeared on my system at least (and with several different servers) that including the OP_HALFOPEN parameter in this function call caused it to always fail when connecting to POP3 servers.  The purpose of the parameter is to make it connect to a mail account only rather than connecting and opening a mailbox. Has anyone else had any luck with using POP3 authentication with the existing code? While I was in there, I added a parameter for configuring the mailbox to connect to (since removing the OP_HALFOPEN makes it require one) rather than hardcoding INBOX.  I also modified a few of the strings that I found confusing.  My modified files are attatched here.  File locations are as follows: /auth/pop3/lib.php /auth/pop3/config.html /lang/en/auth.php

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Disappearing Course Creators
ResponsesInList.Text: OK, got it.... here's the explanation... The auth_iscreator function in ldap.lib checks if the ldap_creator field in the ldap configuration is empty. If so, it simply returns false. But this is wrong, as false means that the routine has identified that the user is *not* a course creator as opposed to the required response that the creator check could not be made (as no value had been placed in the ldap_creator field). The authentication routine back in moodlelib.php takes this at face value and deletes the user's creator record. I think the answer, which I am about to try is to add another function to the auth packages that understand creators to ascertain if the check is possible. Off to code and test it!!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Disappearing Course Creators
ResponsesInList.Text: Ok, here's the fix, line numbers refer to version 1.4.1: In lib/moodlelib.php in function authenticate_user_login, at line 839, immediately *before*: if (function_exists('auth_iscreator') add the following chunk of code: // check if we can do creator check at all $creator_possible=true; if (function_exists('auth_iscreatordefined')) { $creator_possible=auth_iscreatordefined(); } The if (function_exists('auth_iscreator') line now needs to be modified slightly to: if (function_exists('auth_iscreator') && $creator_possible) {    // Check if the user is a creator now in auth/ldap/ldap.lib, at or about line 362, in front of auth_iscreator function definition, add the following new function: function auth_iscreatordefined() { /// check if ldap_creator and ldap_memberattribute are filled in /// required to do creator check return !(($CFG->ldap_creators=="") OR ($CFG->ldap_memberattribute=="")); } checked and working!!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: IMAP stalls on special characters after server upgrade
ResponsesInList.Text:
The system administrators have been so kind as to start up the old mail server. Apparently the old mail server used WU IMAP While the new mail server uses Courier IMAP There is apparently no reason why the login recognition should have stopped at 7pm last night, when we had an access from Western Australia. 218.223.192.34 It seems to be one of our students though. Since that time students have tried to log in 3000 times. But it is working again using the Old server. I am raking the internet for differences between the two IMAPs. This person seems to be having login problems when upgrading from wu to courier, but there does not seem to be a solution on the courier list. http://www.mail-archive.com/courier-users@lists.sourceforge.net/msg04439.html Here is an intriging description of the birth of Courier IMAP from out of WU IMAP and the flame wars between them. http://www.courier-mta.org/fud/ WHere the maker of Courier, Sam Varshavchik writes My response to claims that Courier-IMAP is not a compliant IMAP server is very simple: there was no such thing as a compliant IMAP server, because Crispin's IMAP specification makes that an impossible goal. This is Couriers explanation of why one may not be able to log in. Q: Can't log in A: Check the following `AUTHMODULES` in the `pop3d` configuration file is correct. If the `authdaemon` authentication proxy is used, check the `authdaemonrc` configuration file. Check that `authdaemond` is running. Your authentication modules are properly configured. Some authentication modules have additional configuration files ( `authldap` and 
```text
authmy
sql
```
 ). If you're using `authpam` , you need to configure your PAM library to authenticate the " pop3 " service. This is a separate task, and is specific to your PAM library and operating system. You are using a database -based back-end, such as LDAP or MySQL , and the back-end server is down. You're using maildirs. Courier's POP3 server only supports maildirs ( `$HOME/Maildir` ), it doesn't support mailbox files. The students can log into their mail accounts and the university computers without difficulty usiing the new Courier IMAP server. There is something about Moodle that is compatible with WU-IMAP but not Courier-IMAP, perhaps for the reasons outliked by the maker of Courier above. Tim

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: IMAP stalls on special characters after server upgrade
ResponsesInList.Text: Speaking to myself, as a record of my struggle, in case there are or soon will be other users in the same predicament and since I can not keep the old server running indefinately, I joined the Courier users forum but they had nothing to suggest. The logs on the Courier Server are completely blank apparently, it is as if there is no one trying to access the server. My sysadmin refused to believe that there had been attempts to acccess the courier IMAP server at first. But the logs in Moodle show 3000 access attempts, and as soon as the WU was back up, and I changed the server url to match, we were able to login immediately. Looking at the lines in the imap/lib.php that connect to the server... switch ($CFG->auth_imaptype) { case "imapssl": $ host = '{'.$host.":$CFG->auth_imapport/imap/ssl}"; break; case "imapcert": $host = '{'.$host.":$CFG->auth_imapport/imap/ssl/novalidate-cert}"; break; case "imaptls": $host = '{'.$host.":$CFG->auth_imapport/imap/notls}"; break; default: $host = '{'.$host.":$CFG->auth_imapport}"; } $connection = imap_open($host, $username, $password, OP_HALFOPEN); Possibilities 1) Looking at the above code it seems to me that the above it seems to me that the most likely reason is that the path to the business end of the Courier IMAP server is different to that of the WU IMAP server. I have tried all the above settings imap.myunidomain.ac.jp/imap/ssl imap.myunidomain.ac.jp/imap/ssl/novalidate-cert imap.myunidomain.ac.jp/imap/notls imap.myunidomain.ac.jp Perhaps courier imap is different? 2) The "OP_HALFOPEN" was added fairly recently, I am not sure why. I think it is because we are not accessing the mail, just using the IMAP server as a password recognition device. I have not tried changing this yet, because I think that is not there in one of my older moodle installations. 3) Looking on the net I see that this line is sometimes @imap_open but I tried that and it seemed to make no difference (I could still log into WU but not Courier). 4) The database we are using stores things in EUC-JP format I believe. I am not sure if this makes any difference with password and username fields, which do not have any Japanese, just roman letters in them, but perhaps it does. For a while the access to the Courier server half-worked. That is to say that most people were able to access the server but somepeople, with special characters, particularly "}" in their usernames were not able to login. As far as I am aware, special characters have different character codes, while the alphabetical characters do not. So perhaps I should add $host = mb_convert_encoding($host, "EUC-JP", "ASCII"); THIS DID NOT WORK Or perhaps since their are squiggly brackets around the domain name and these are most likely causing the problem perhaps there is some way of specifying and adding them using their ascii code directly? 5) Perhaps when connecting to Courier IMAP the domain should not be contained in squiggly brackets as above. Hmm. What are the {} doing there? Anyway, something is different between WU and Courier servers but I am not sure what. Tim Takemoto

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: IMAP stalls on special characters after server upgrade
ResponsesInList.Text: Hmm, it now works. I guess that the system administrator did something. Thinking that it was me, I wrote the following. The problem seems to have been the encoding. I had the above encoding conversion the wrong way around. It should be $host = mb_convert_encoding($host, "ASCII", "EUC-JP"); Adding this just before the connection works, but I guess this is of no relevance to those that are not using EUC-JP, and (for all I know) it may even prevent IMAP login from working if the string being converted is not in EUC-JP. So, how about this... switch ($CFG->auth_imaptype) { case "imapssl": $host = $host.":$CFG->auth_imapport/imap/ssl"; break; case "imapcert": $host = $host.":$CFG->auth_imapport/imap/ssl/novalidate-cert"; break; case "imaptls": $host = $host.":$CFG->auth_imapport/imap/notls"; break; default: $host = $host.":$CFG->auth_imapport"; } $host = chr(123).$host.chr(125); // adds the squiggles as ascii characters. The above also works and there is no mention of EUC-JP. It also may even be marginally shorter than the original. I am just making sure that the squiggles are being added as ascii and not EUC-JP characters. I am not sure why Courier should be less tolerant than WU but that is just the way it is. But wait, space goats, doing this also works... $host = "{".$host."}"; er??? Putting the file back to what it was an hour ago works!!! The system adminstrator must have done something. Tim

ResponsesInList.Title: Performance fix for LDAP's user_sync()
ResponsesInList.Text: If you are using auth/ldap, and have a large userbase, running user_sync() (usually from a short custom script, here called cron.php) takes _ages_. On my fast dev server , with 4k users, it takes ~8 minutes. Disregard the low user time -- this is nailing mysql for 6 solid minutes: $ time php cron.php real 7m47.537s user 1m7.550s sys 0m5.420s With a bit of trickery and magic, I've mananged to get it down to 2 minutes, and now the process is php-bound: $ time php cron.php real 1m54.598s

ResponsesInList.Title: Authentication methods and administrators
ResponsesInList.Text: Finally worked out what was phasing me with authentication methods. Administrators are 'forced' to use only the internal authentication methods - all administrators (line 770 in moodlelib.php). That's why a user created manually (or probably by any method) will always be able to log in after the auth method is changed ONLY if they are an administrator. Ordinary users will no longer be able to login if the method is changed of course. This is why I thought that users that had already been created continued to work after we had swapped to LDAP (we had quite a few admins), and this confused the hell out of me. But... its seems to be that the downside of this is that if I promote an LDAP user to administrator, their LDAP login details will from then on be completely ignored. If their password is changed in the LDAP database it will not be reflected in Moodle. Is this a bug or a feature? I am working in this area at the moment to make it so manual authorisation is always available, and I'd like to get some opinions on this one.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Authentication methods and administrators
ResponsesInList.Text: It's a feature - a safeguard in case the other method of authentication doesn't work. For example, when you are configuring authentication for a new Moodle installation, it can happen that you screw up. In that case, without this safeguard, you wouldn't be able to log in and correct your mistake.  And it is not true that the password won't be updated. If the administrator logs in with their newly changed LDAP password, their login will be accepted, and the local password will be updated to reflect this. The logic goes as follows: Try the local password first. This fails, so try LDAP next. This succeeds, so the administrator is logged in. After every successful login, the local password is updated with the one used for the successful login, in this case the new LDAP password. So the only possible problem is if you think that an administrator's password has been compromised. In that case, you need to remember not only to change the LDAP password, but also to login to Moodle with the new password.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Authentication methods and administrators
ResponsesInList.Text: mmmm...... I don't agree. If an administrator's password is changed in LDAP (perhaps, for example, because you want to keep them out) and they log in with their old password - they *still* get into Moodle. Yes, they would be able to log in with their new LDAP password because *then* the local password will fail, but the point is that changing the LDAP password will not prevent a user logging in (with the existing password). Is this good security? Does it matter? I'm not sure, but it's certainly counter-intuitive. My take would be to make it so that only the 'master' administrator gets this privilege, as they must have been created manually any way.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Authentication methods and administrators
ResponsesInList.Text: No.  Unless something has recently changed in weblib.php, in your hypothetical case of a rogue administrator, you just need an extra step to lock him out.  Namely (1) first change his LDAP password, then (2) log in as him with the new password.  Step (2) will purge his old password from the local Moodle database.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Authentication methods and administrators
ResponsesInList.Text: In the new system, if you add a user manually, then the "auth" field in the "user" table will be set to "manual".  Therefore LDAP or other methods won't be checked or used, regardless of whether the user is an admin or not.  The primary admin will ALWAYS be "manual" so that safety precaution is preserved. If you allow LDAP users, then their "auth" field will be "ldap", even if you promote them to being admins.  Their login details will always be treated as external, and the internal copy of the password will NEVER be used.   So this covers your rogue admin. Everyone happy with this?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MD5 Revisited
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Pablo, two things about your problem: 1. What you have is not a complete solution for the issue. It does prevent anyone from learning your cleartext (unencrypted) passwords, but it doesn't prevent them from storing the exchange between your browser and the server and later playing it back to gain access to the system (this is called a replay attack). To defeat a replay attack, you will need to do a couple of more things: first, when a new session is created, the server assigns a random number as session variable. The server sends this to the browser, in the form of a hidden input field (let's call this number randval ). The hidden field has the value md5(randval) , which we will call randhash . Then, when the user clicks submit, you don't send back md5(password) but instead: md5(md5(password) + randhash) == md5(md5(password) + md5(randval)) . From the server side, you know md5(password) and randval, so you can compute md5(randval) and then md5(md5(password) + md5(randval)). Check for equality with what the browser sent you and you have secure authentication. The advantage of this technique is that even if someone eavesdrops on the connection and gains access to the data transmitted, when the legitimate user's session ends and someone later tries to reconnect, the server will assign a different randval, so the randhash will be different and thus a replay attack (using an old and "wrong" randhash) will fail. 2. What you do in your script is set the value of the password to something. What you have to do instead is include a hidden input field (for example md5pass) and do: md5pass = md5(md5(password) + randhash); password = ''; before submitting. This brings the following advantages: Browsers don't give you trouble with their password managers (because on the server side you don't check the value of password at all, you use md5pass) The password disappears from screen when the user clicks submit, which is prettier than having it expand to 32 characters. Hope this helps you solve your problems! Jon

ResponsesInList.Title: LDAP 2307 Authentication Module
ResponsesInList.Text: I ran into a problem in setting up our instance of Moodle while trying to get the LDAP authentication module to work completely. While I had no problems pointing it to our directory server and having users authenticate, I ran into problems with the automatic granting of course creator status. Digging into the code, I found that the current LDAP authentication module expects that the user's LDAP object contains attributes that specify the groups of which a user is a member. Our directory is set up slightly differently: group objects contain attributes that list the members of the group. This is apparently a fairly common way of organizing a directory, at least to those of us that come from the Unix and NIS universe (it's exactly the same concept as the Unix /etc/passwd and /etc/group files). In order to make creator status work with our directory, I wrote a new LDAP module based on the current one, but with a significantly altered auth_iscreator() function that looks up the group objects that contain attributes listing the currently logged in user (I also added the helper function auth_ldap_get_grouplist()). As our account management is done entirely outside the scope of Moodle, I also removed the user creation, activation, and disabling functions of the original LDAP module. Rather than make these changes to the original LDAP module, I thought that the groups structure represented a fundamental enough conceptual departure to warrant a completely separate module, at least to start out. (I certainly wouldn't be adverse to folding the two back together at some point.) The new module is called ldap2307, after the RFC number that contains this directory structure specification. I consider this module to be completely functional and stable, however it has had a limited testing environment. I have tested it in Moodle v1.1.1 and the current 1.2 beta against a Sun ONE directory server, and a colleague has tested it against OpenLDAP. We've found no problems with the code as it currently stands, although it's entirely possible that you'll have a local configuration that exposes a "gotcha". In the attached ZIP file, there is the ldap2307 authentication module and two language files: auth.php.new and auth.php.diff. The .new is a complete version of the lang/en/auth.php file with text for this module added. The .diff file is a "diff" against the original lang/en/auth.php file in Moodle v1.2 beta; you can apply it to your version with the Unix "patch" command.

The solution is to place the instructions into a standard php file containing string variable(s) and to draw them from there. 2) In the directory '/lang/[chosen_language]' create a new file (e.g. 'my_login.php'). 3) Place your instructions in there: <?php $string['myloginsteps'] = 'The text of your instructions, don \ 't forget to use backslash in front of single and double quotation marks. You can use HTML.'; ?> 4) Edit the file '/login/index_form.html'. Find the switch ($CFG->auth) expression and insert a new case for the switch after case "none" : case "none":

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle integrated into a High School Intranet
ResponsesInList.Text: The computing faculty at our High School is currently revamping the student and staff Intranet with the aim of developing an interactive and collaborative teaching and learning environment. Our efforts are based around applications from the open source PHP community. We have implemented 'phpbb2' as our forum base, 'mambo' as our articles, subject resources, news and general Intranet interface and now I am investigating moodle as the online provider of (enrichment to begin with) courses. As we have a captive clientle, we authenticate each user in the applications against the same database (so during registration they choose from a drop down list of their uptodate Novell account usernames), this also allows their photo etc to be automatically included in the different apps and postings. This also allows personalisation of the sites based on the user being either a staff member or a student. Eg. staff can post and access learning resources whereas students can only access them (for obvious reasons). OK. We can provide the technology, but have yet to grapple with the elements of training of staff, changing the culture of learning to a more collaborative and sharing one, and in the case of moodle, what content is appropriate, within Dept guidelines etc. Any thoughts, suggestions, approaches etc? environment is: State High School,867 pop. Co-ed NSW, Australia

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle integrated into a High School Intranet

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle integrated into a High School Intranet
ResponsesInList.Text: Martin you wrote "I'm not sure what the problem is with content and department guidelines - I would assume that's up to individual teachers. Can you explain that further?" -- I was refering to the fact that we are to follow the syllabus and outcomes as provided by the NSW dept of school ed. Approval to post full HSC courses online from a school, would need to be sought from above. Early stages as yet for this.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle integrated into a High School Intranet
ResponsesInList.Text: Martin I have posted up a course in Information Technology for year 12 students, as part of a 2 year course, including resources (theory notes) , assignments based on competencies, quizes to test the competencies, forum and a journal.  The student response is interesting! As they are all "into computing" anyway they enjoy using the application you have developed and majority of these students are also software programming students who are into php, so they are following the development of moodle with furvour.  The learning atmosphere in the classroom has changed dramatically. Students are very self directed (clear goals and deadlines) but remarkably the students have responded to using journals to document their daily progress on the unit of work. Some have used the journals to store study notes for their later use.  The effect of "1 day 12 hours" to go for an assignment has achieved 100% compliance rate ( a 1st)  --- I felt "displaced"  for a while as my role mutated slightly (the need for chalk & talk is engrained). The students responded well to the immediate feedback given to assignments and journal. The issue remains of dealing with students who finish the unit a lot earlier than others - do they progress to the next unit or extension work etc.  The amount of non productive work (social internet access etc.) has dramatically decreased - is it that they are using the computers anyway in a directed manner? Staff are very enthusiastic about their Course in Computing Applications - a good sign. Generally, the introduction of moodle has recieved rave reviews throughout the school. The journal concept has attracted most interest - students actually keep them up to date, a most unexpected thing in a secondary school. I am investigating a new module for non assessable (no grade book entry) activities that can enhance the learning experience.  Thank you for your work - the quiz module is a masterpiece on a global scale.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle integrated into a High School Intranet
ResponsesInList.Text: Alan, Thank you very much for that - it's terrific for me to hear stories of Moodle being used out there.  Particularly such positive ones! PHP programming can be great fun as you sometimes get a lot of effect for a little effort (then again sometimes you get little effect for a lot of effort) ... sounds like you have some budding hackers there (not crackers, hopefully). I'm very interested to hear more about how you have used the journals ... did you use few or many?  When I designed it I was planning for each journal entry to be quite short, and that teachers would set up one or two journal activities in every week.  Since then I've found many people are using only one or two of them in a whole course, and encouraging repeat visits so that they build up one big entry over a long time.  As a result I'm thinking of new ideas for the journal to make it more dialogical, like a private forum between student and teacher. Glad you like the quiz module ... it was my most frequent request and I put a lot of work into it.  Since it's now released mostly all I've heard is requests for new things instead. One more thing - are you using the LDAP authentication? Cheers, Martin

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Novell usernames
ResponsesInList.Text: Martin; We used NDS Exporter ( http://prope.insa-lyon.fr/~ppollet/netware/ ) freeware which extracts any NDS field out of NDs into delimited file, then put it into a db table to be queried at leisure. Moodle (in high school situation) needs to have the Novell login name , fullname in a comma delimited format sent as a variable username then split it up into its components either side of the comma using the php split function. You now have the novell login name and novell fullname at your disposal. We use this in the drop down selection boxes in the registration area so students can only use there novell login names (eg. 04kel) as the username in an application. No option to change name in "details" or "profile" is allowed.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Novell usernames
ResponsesInList.Text: Does the Novell export include passwords too? And are you saying that your other apps have a drop-down selection menu containing ALL student names? (that could be huge!) My current plan for integrating this stuff into Moodle is as follows: Admin selects "external source" for usernames, and the source type (SOAP lookup, database table etc). When user types in their username and password to log in), Moodle first checks it against the external source. If the username/password were correct, Moodle creates or updates a local entry in the user table (which in addition to the external username/password contains all the extra Moodle fields like picture, email, etc etc). If the username didn't exist on the source then any local copy is also wiped and access is denied. Lastly, if the user attempts to change their username or password then Moodle forwards them to an admin-defined external URL to do it (eg Novell). How does that sound?
